lesson.title: Relative Fitness: Success Is Relative, Not Absolute
lesson.summary: In evolutionary biology, fitness is not about strength or health but about how many surviving, reproducing offspring a genotype leaves compared with other genotypes in the same population.
lesson.body:
In everyday language, calling something fit suggests strong, healthy, or athletic. In evolutionary biology, fitness has a much narrower and more precise meaning, directly building on the process of natural selection described in the previous chapter. Fitness is a measure of reproductive success, specifically how many viable, fertile offspring an individual, or more precisely a genotype, contributes to the next generation, compared with other individuals or genotypes in that same population. It is called relative fitness because it is always measured relative to other members of the population, not against any absolute standard of health or strength. A genotype can have high fitness while producing an organism that looks physically unimpressive, and low fitness while producing one that looks robust, what matters is reproductive output, not appearance.

Biologists often express this by assigning the genotype with the highest reproductive success in a given environment a relative fitness value of one, with other genotypes assigned lower values in proportion to how many fewer offspring they contribute on average. Relative fitness is typically discussed at the level of genotype, since it is the genotype, not the phenotype alone, that gets transmitted to offspring. But the causal chain runs through phenotype, an individual's genotype produces its phenotype, that phenotype interacts with the environment to determine survival and reproductive success, and that success is what relative fitness actually measures. The result then feeds back to change genotype frequencies in the next generation, which is exactly how natural selection operates over time.

A genotype's relative fitness is not a fixed, permanent property, it depends entirely on the environment it is measured in. The classic example is the sickle cell allele in humans. Carrying two copies of this allele causes sickle cell disease, which lowers fitness in essentially any environment. But carrying just one copy, alongside one normal allele, provides meaningful resistance to malaria, which can give heterozygous individuals a relative fitness advantage over both homozygous genotypes specifically in regions where malaria is common. The same allele is favored in one environment and strongly disfavored in another, which is exactly why fitness has to be understood as relative to a specific population in a specific environment, not as some fixed, universal property of a gene.

Natural selection lets the environment determine which genotypes end up with the highest relative fitness. The next chapter examines what happens when a different force takes over that role entirely, human choice.
